title: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
summary: How speech becomes log-mel spectrograms, how Whisper's encoder-decoder and CTC models like wav2vec 2.0 turn them into text, how WER is computed and normalized, and how long-form, streaming and silence go wrong.
outcomes: Compute frame counts and mel values for a log-mel front end with a 25 ms window and 10 ms hop
Explain how Whisper maps 30 s of audio to 3000 frames and 1500 encoder positions, and how tokens specify the task
Collapse a CTC path and explain how wav2vec 2.0 learns from unlabeled audio before CTC fine-tuning
Compute WER from an alignment table and explain why text normalization changes it
Diagnose long-form drift, streaming latency and hallucination on silence, and pick mitigations

lessons.title: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram

blocks.md:
A microphone signal for speech recognition is usually stored at 16 kHz: 16,000 numbers per second, so a 10 second voice note is 160,000 numbers. The same word spoken louder, faster or by a different voice gives a completely different list of samples, and a tiny time shift changes every value.

What stays stable is *which frequencies carry energy* and how that pattern moves over time. From the signal processing prerequisite you know the DFT turns a block of samples into a spectrum. Speech recognizers apply it to many short, overlapping blocks and stack the results into a picture of frequency over time: a spectrogram.

The standard recipe, used by Whisper, cuts the audio into **frames**:

- **Window**: 25 ms of audio, which is 400 samples at 16 kHz.
- **Hop** (also called stride): the next frame starts 10 ms (160 samples) later, so neighbouring frames overlap by 15 ms.
- Each frame is multiplied by a Hann window (to reduce spectral leakage) and sent through an FFT of size 400, giving 201 frequency bins spaced 16000 / 400 = 40 Hz apart.

The squared magnitude of each bin is the frame's power spectrum. One frame becomes one column of the spectrogram.

blocks.title: 25 ms windows sliding by 10 ms hops

scenes.caption: Frame 0 covers 0 to 25 ms of audio: 400 samples at 16 kHz.
Frame 1 starts one hop (10 ms) later. The two frames share 15 ms of audio, so a sound that straddles a frame edge is still seen whole by some frame.
Every 10 ms a new frame starts. The frame rate is set by the hop, not the window: 100 frames per second.
Doubling the window to 50 ms would make each frame longer (finer frequency resolution, blurrier timing) but frames would still start every 10 ms.

blocks.prompt: How many frames do you get from exactly 1 s of 16 kHz audio with a 25 ms window and a 10 ms hop?
blocks.reveal:
It depends on padding, and the difference matters when you line up shapes.

- **No padding**: the last frame must fit inside the signal, so $1 + \lfloor (16000 - 400)/160 \rfloor = 1 + 97 = 98$ frames.
- **Centered** (librosa and `torch.stft` with `center=True` pad 200 samples on each side so frame $t$ is centered at $t \times 160$): $1 + \lfloor 16000/160 \rfloor = 101$ frames.

Whisper uses the centered STFT and then drops the last frame (`stft[..., :-1]` in its code), so it gets exactly 100 frames per second and **3000 frames for 30 s**.

blocks.caption: N samples, window W samples, hop H samples. For N = 16000, W = 400, H = 160 these give 98 and 101.

blocks.md:
The FFT bins are evenly spaced in Hz, but human pitch perception is not: the step from 100 Hz to 200 Hz sounds much bigger than the step from 7,000 Hz to 7,100 Hz. The **mel scale** warps frequency so equal mel steps are closer to equal perceived steps. Two versions are in common use:

- **HTK**: $m = 2595 \log_{10}(1 + f/700)$.
- **Slaney** (librosa's default): linear below 1000 Hz ($m = 3f/200$, so 1000 Hz is 15 mel), logarithmic above ($m = 15 + 27 \ln(f/1000) / \ln 6.4$).

For 0, 1000, 4000 and 8000 Hz, HTK gives 0, 1000, 2146 and 2840 mel. Slaney gives 0, 15, 35.16 and 45.25 mel. The units differ, but the shape is similar.

blocks.title: How the mel scale squeezes high frequencies

y.label: Fraction of the 0 to 8 kHz mel range

scenes.caption: On a linear axis, 0 to 1000 Hz is only 12.5% of the range up to 8 kHz.
On the HTK mel scale the same 0 to 1000 Hz takes 35% of the range, and half the mel axis is spent below about 1768 Hz.
Slaney's version is exactly linear up to 1000 Hz (33% of its range) and logarithmic above. 4 to 8 kHz gets only 22% of the axis, versus 50% on a linear axis.

blocks.md:
A **mel filterbank** turns the 201 FFT bins into a few dozen bands. It places triangle-shaped filters at centers evenly spaced on the mel axis, and each band's value is a weighted sum of the power in the bins under its triangle. Whisper uses 80 bands from 0 to 8000 Hz built by `librosa.filters.mel(sr=16000, n_fft=400, n_mels=80)` (Slaney scale). With that scale, 26 of the 80 band centers sit below 1000 Hz. The lowest band is about 75 Hz wide and the highest about 590 Hz wide.

Finally the power is put on a log scale, because loudness perception and the dynamic range of speech are closer to logarithmic. Whisper's code takes log10, clips everything more than 8 (that is, 80 dB) below the loudest value, then rescales.

blocks.caption: Whisper's log-mel normalization, from log_mel_spectrogram in whisper/audio.py. P is the mel-band power; the result lands roughly in [-1, 1].

blocks.title: A toy log-mel spectrogram: silence, a low tone, a high tone

scenes.caption: Simplified: 8 mel bands instead of 80, every 5th frame shown (labels are frame times in ms). 0 to 200 ms is near-silence, 200 to 400 ms is 300 Hz plus 600 Hz, then a 2500 Hz tone.
The low tones light the 335 Hz and 670 Hz bands. Columns 200 to 350 ms carry the same pattern, which is what makes the representation stable for a held sound.
After 400 ms the energy jumps to the bands centered at 2008 Hz and 2836 Hz, the two triangles that overlap 2500 Hz.
Frames centered at 200 ms and 400 ms straddle a change, so their 25 ms windows mix both sounds and the sharp edges smear energy across many bands.

blocks.md: A log-mel spectrogram is 80 numbers every 10 ms. Whisper's 30 second input is therefore an 80 x 3000 matrix: the model never sees raw samples.

Mel settings are not interchangeable. librosa defaults to the Slaney scale, while `torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram` defaults to `mel_scale='htk'` and `n_mels=128`. Features computed with different settings than a model was trained on look like a different microphone to the model.

blocks.question: Which single change halves the number of spectrogram frames per second?
options: Increase the window from 25 ms to 50 ms
Increase the hop from 10 ms to 20 ms
Reduce the mel bands from 80 to 40
Resample from 16 kHz to 8 kHz but keep a 25 ms window and 10 ms hop
blocks.explain: Frames per second is 1 / hop, so a 20 ms hop gives 50 frames per second. A longer window makes each frame cover more time but they still start every 10 ms. Fewer mel bands makes each column shorter, not the sequence. Resampling changes samples per frame, not frames per second.

blocks.question: On the Slaney mel scale, which span covers more mel units: 0 to 1000 Hz or 4000 to 8000 Hz?
options: 0 to 1000 Hz (15 mel versus about 10.1 mel)
4000 to 8000 Hz, because it is four times wider in Hz
They are equal, because the scale is logarithmic everywhere
It depends on the number of mel bands
blocks.explain: 0 to 1000 Hz is the linear part: 15 mel. 4000 to 8000 Hz is one doubling in the log region: 27 ln 2 / ln 6.4, about 10.1 mel. So the filterbank spends more bands on the lowest kilohertz, where vowels and pitch live, than on the top four kilohertz. The number of bands only decides how finely the axis is cut.

lessons.title: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows

blocks.md:
Before Whisper, the strongest English recognizers were trained on curated datasets such as LibriSpeech (read audiobooks). They reach very low error on that test set but degrade sharply on phone calls, meetings or accented speech. The Whisper paper (Radford et al., OpenAI, 2022) bet on **weak supervision at scale** instead: **680,000 hours** of audio paired with transcripts found on the internet, of which 117,000 hours cover 96 languages other than English and 125,000 hours are translation pairs from other languages into English.

The transcripts are noisy, so the team filtered heavily, for example removing transcripts that looked machine-generated by existing ASR systems, and then trained a standard model without dataset-specific fine-tuning.

The model is an off-the-shelf **encoder-decoder transformer** (the architecture from the attention prerequisite), chosen so results reflect data and scale rather than new architecture tricks:

1. Resample audio to 16 kHz and pad or trim it to 30 s (480,000 samples).
2. Compute the 80 x 3000 log-mel spectrogram.
3. A **conv stem**: two 1D convolutions of width 3 with GELU, the second with stride 2.
4. Add sinusoidal position embeddings, then run the encoder blocks.
5. The decoder predicts text tokens (GPT-2 byte-level BPE, refit for the multilingual models) and reads the encoder output through cross-attention.

scenes.caption: Any input is padded or trimmed to exactly 30 s, so the encoder always sees the same shape.
The second convolution has stride 2, halving the time axis. Each encoder position now stands for 20 ms of audio.
The decoder is a language model conditioned on audio: each step attends to all 1500 encoder outputs and predicts the next token.

blocks.prompt: The encoder stem turns 3000 mel frames into how many positions, and what does one position represent in time?
blocks.reveal:
Conv 1 has width 3, padding 1, stride 1, so it keeps 3000 positions. Conv 2 has stride 2: $\lfloor (3000 + 2 - 3)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 1500$ positions.

30 s / 1500 = **20 ms per position**. That is why the paper quantizes timestamps to 20 ms, "the native time resolution of Whisper models". It also makes encoder self-attention cheaper: its score matrix is $1500^2$ instead of $3000^2$, 4x fewer entries.

blocks.caption: Convolution output length for kernel k, padding p, stride s. Whisper's code uses k = 3, p = 1 for both layers, and s = 1 then s = 2.

blocks.md:
One decoder handles many tasks because the **task is written in the prompt**. After `<|startoftranscript|>` the model predicts a language token (99 languages), or `<|nospeech|>` if the window has no speech. Then comes `<|transcribe|>` or `<|translate|>` (translation is always into English), then either `<|notimestamps|>` or timestamp tokens.

Timestamps are tokens too: times relative to the window, quantized to 20 ms, with a start time before each caption segment and an end time after it. With some probability, training also puts the previous window's transcript before the prompt as context, and the loss on that context is masked.

blocks.title: Whisper's decoder sequence for one window

scenes.caption: Simplified: words stand in for BPE tokens, and the times are illustrative. SOT is the start-of-transcript token, EOT the end token.
After the start token, the next two predictions fix language and task. At inference you can force them (for example language en, task transcribe) instead of letting the model guess.
Timestamp tokens bracket each segment: start 0.00 s, then the text, then the end time. These are what long-form transcription later uses to move the window.
Spanish audio with the translate task: the language token says es, but the text comes out in English. Same weights, different prompt.
A window with no speech: the target is the no-speech token right after start, followed by the end token.
Parameters in millions: 39M to 1550M. Encoder and decoder have the same width and depth.
Transformer layers per stack: 4, 6, 12, 24, 32, with widths 384 to 1280. Bigger models are slower but more accurate.

blocks.md:
Training used AdamW, batches of 256 thirty-second segments and $2^{20}$ updates, only two to three passes over the data, with no data augmentation in the original models (the later Large V2 added SpecAugment and other regularization).

Weak labels leave fingerprints. Early models guessed **speaker names**, because many web transcripts include them even though the name is rarely inferable from 30 s of audio. The authors removed this by briefly fine-tuning on transcripts without speaker annotations. Keep this in mind for lesson 5: a decoder trained on web text will write what web text tends to contain.

Whisper is an audio-conditioned language model. The encoder turns 30 s of log-mel into 1500 vectors; the decoder generates the transcript token by token, with language, task and timestamps expressed as tokens in the same sequence.

blocks.question: You pass 12 s of audio to Whisper. What does the encoder process?
options: A 80 x 1200 spectrogram, 600 positions
A 80 x 3000 spectrogram, 1500 positions, with the last 18 s padded with zeros
Three 4 s chunks processed in parallel
The raw 192,000 samples directly
blocks.explain: Whisper always feeds the encoder 30 s: the low-level API pads the audio to 480,000 samples, and `transcribe` pads each log-mel window to 3000 frames, so the shape is always 80 x 3000 and the stem always yields 1500 positions. The padded tail is silence, which matters later when we look at hallucinations.

blocks.question: Whisper's timestamp tokens are quantized to the native resolution. A word starts at 1.234 s. What is the closest timestamp the model can emit?
blocks.explain: Each encoder position covers 20 ms (30 s / 1500), and timestamp tokens are on the same 20 ms grid: ..., 1.22, 1.24, ... The nearest grid point to 1.234 s is 1.24 s. Finer word timings need extra machinery, such as the cross-attention alignment the openai/whisper code offers for word timestamps.

lessons.title: CTC and wav2vec 2.0: training without frame-level alignments

blocks.md:
Whisper's decoder writes text freely. An older and still widely used design attaches a classifier to **every encoder frame** instead. That raises an alignment problem: one second of audio gives about 50 encoder frames, but the word *hello* has 5 letters, and nobody labeled which frames belong to which letter.

Earlier neural systems needed pre-segmented training data (a label for every frame) plus post-processing to turn frame outputs into text. **Connectionist Temporal Classification** (CTC, Graves, Fernández, Gomez and Schmidhuber, ICML 2006) removes that need: the network outputs, at each frame, a probability for every label plus an extra **blank** label, and training sums over every alignment that spells the right answer.

CTC defines a many-to-one map $\mathcal{B}$ from a frame-level path to a label sequence: **first merge repeated labels, then remove blanks**. The paper's example: $\mathcal{B}(a{-}ab{-}) = \mathcal{B}({-}aa{-}{-}abb) = aab$, where $-$ is the blank.

Repeats let one letter last for several frames. Blanks let the model say nothing during silence or transitions, and they are the only way to emit the same letter twice in a row.

blocks.title: CTC collapse: merge repeats, then drop blanks

scenes.caption: Per-frame best labels for 12 frames (_ is the blank). Most frames are blanks or repeats: CTC outputs tend to be short spikes separated by blanks.
Step 1 merges runs: hh becomes h, oo becomes o. The two l runs stay separate because a blank sits between them.
Step 2 removes blanks and yields hello. Many different paths collapse to the same text, and CTC training adds up all their probabilities.
Bug: with no blank between the l frames (lll), merging keeps one l and the output is helo. A double letter always needs a blank between its copies.

blocks.caption: CTC likelihood (Graves et al. 2006): sum over every frame path that collapses to the label sequence l, where y is the per-frame softmax. A forward-backward dynamic program computes it efficiently.

blocks.md:
Two consequences follow from this formula. First, frame outputs are **conditionally independent** given the input: the model has no built-in way to make letter choices depend on earlier output letters, so CTC systems often add an external language model during decoding. Second, each output is tied to a frame, so a CTC model can emit text as frames arrive whenever its encoder does not need much future audio.

The simplest decoder, **best path decoding**, takes the top label per frame and collapses it, exactly as in the figure. The paper notes this is not guaranteed to find the most probable label sequence, because that probability is spread over many paths.

blocks.question: A CTC model must output the word too. Which frame path collapses to too?
options: t o o
t t o o o
t o _ o
_ t o o _
blocks.explain: Merging repeats turns t o o, t t o o o and _ t o o _ into to (or _to_, then to). Only t o _ o keeps two separate o runs, because the blank breaks the run before merging. Removing the blank then gives too.

blocks.md:
CTC still needs labeled audio, and most of the world's roughly 7,000 languages have little of it. **wav2vec 2.0** (Baevski, Zhou, Mohamed and Auli, Facebook AI, 2020) first learns from **unlabeled** audio, then fine-tunes with CTC on a small labeled set.

Its parts:

- A **CNN feature encoder** on the raw waveform: 7 conv blocks with strides (5,2,2,2,2,2,2) and kernel widths (10,3,3,3,3,2,2). The total stride is 320 samples, about 20 ms, with a 25 ms receptive field.
- A **transformer context network** on top of those latents.
- A **quantization module** that maps each latent to a discrete code (product quantization with G = 2 codebooks of V = 320 entries, chosen with a Gumbel softmax).

blocks.title: wav2vec 2.0: mask latents, then pick the true code

scenes.caption: The CNN turns raw samples into one latent vector about every 20 ms (49 per second).
Pre-training masks spans of latents before the transformer: each step is a span start with probability 0.065, and a span covers 10 steps. About half of all steps end up masked.
The quantizer sees the unmasked latents. For each masked step the context vector must pick the true quantized code among 101 candidates: the target plus 100 distractors from other masked steps.
Fine-tuning drops the quantizer and adds a linear layer over 29 character tokens plus a word boundary, trained with CTC on labeled audio.

blocks.prompt: wav2vec 2.0's encoder applies no padding. How many latent frames does 1 s of 16 kHz audio produce?
blocks.reveal: Apply $\lfloor (L - k)/s \rfloor + 1$ layer by layer: 16000, then 3199, 1599, 799, 399, 199, 99 and finally **49**. That matches the paper's "49 hz" encoder output frequency, slightly below 50 because each layer trims its edges.

blocks.caption: Left: the contrastive loss with cosine similarity and temperature kappa (a diversity loss is added to use all codebook entries). Right: a quick estimate of the masked fraction, matching the paper's 'approximately 49%'.

blocks.md: The payoff is label efficiency. With all 960 labeled hours of LibriSpeech, wav2vec 2.0 reached 1.8 / 3.3 WER on test-clean / test-other. Pre-trained on 53,000 hours of unlabeled LibriVox audio and fine-tuned on just **ten minutes** of labeled speech, it still reached 4.8 / 8.2. With one labeled hour it beat the previous best result on the 100 hour subset while using 100 times less labeled data.

Two families: CTC models (like wav2vec 2.0 fine-tuned) classify every frame and collapse the path, so output is tied to audio frames. Encoder-decoder models (like Whisper) generate text with a decoder that also acts as a language model, which buys punctuation and multitask prompts and brings language-model failure modes such as loops.

blocks.question: During wav2vec 2.0 pre-training, what does the model have to identify at a masked time step?
options: The raw waveform samples under the mask
The transcript character spoken at that moment
The true quantized latent for that step, among K distractors
The log-mel spectrogram of the next frame
blocks.explain: Pre-training uses no transcripts. The context vector c_t must score the true quantized latent q_t above 100 distractors sampled from other masked steps of the same utterance. Characters only enter later, during CTC fine-tuning.

lessons.title: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons

blocks.md:
**Word error rate** (WER) is the standard ASR metric. Align the system's output (the *hypothesis*) to the human *reference* transcript with the fewest word edits, then count:

- **S** substitutions (a reference word replaced by a different word),
- **D** deletions (a reference word missing),
- **I** insertions (an extra word in the hypothesis).

Divide by **N**, the number of words in the reference. The alignment is the word-level edit distance (Levenshtein distance) computed with dynamic programming.

blocks.caption: N counts reference words only, so insertions can push WER above 1.

blocks.md: A worked example. Reference: *please set an alarm for six* (N = 6). Hypothesis: *set an alarm far six now*. A word-by-word comparison by position would say almost everything is wrong, because the dropped first word shifts everything. The alignment finds a cheaper explanation.

blocks.title: Edit distance table: reference rows, hypothesis columns

scenes.caption: Cell (i, j) is the fewest edits that turn the first i reference words into the first j hypothesis words. The first row and column count pure insertions or deletions.
Each cell is the minimum of: diagonal + 0 if the words match (+1 if not), up + 1 (deletion), left + 1 (insertion). The bottom-right cell, 3, is the total edit count.
Tracing back the cheapest route: down for please (deletion), diagonals for set an alarm, a diagonal +1 for for vs far, a diagonal for six, then right for now (insertion).
The aligned pair, with - marking a gap. Reading column by column gives the edit operations.
Four columns match (C). Correct words cost nothing.
for became far: one substitution (S). Acoustically close words are the classic substitution.
please has no partner: one deletion (D). now has no reference word: one insertion (I).
S = 1, D = 1, I = 1, N = 6, so WER = 3 / 6 = 50%. The insertion counts in the numerator, but the denominator only counts reference words.

blocks.prompt: Can WER exceed 100%? Try reference *hi there* and hypothesis *hi hi there there you*.
blocks.reveal: Yes. The best alignment matches hi and there and inserts three words, so S = 0, D = 0, I = 3 and N = 2: WER = 3 / 2 = **150%**. A system that babbles or loops can score far above 100%, which is one reason a hallucinating long-form transcript can wreck an average.

blocks.md:
WER compares strings, so it also punishes differences no listener would care about. With whitespace splitting, reference *Hello, Dr. Lee.* and hypothesis *hello doctor lee* score **100%** (three substitutions). After lowercasing, stripping punctuation and expanding *Dr.* to *doctor*, they score **0%**.

The Whisper paper calls this out: a zero-shot model never saw each dataset's transcript conventions, so the authors built a text normalizer by inspecting where naive WER penalized innocuous differences. On some datasets it lowered WER by up to 50%, often because of quirks such as references that split contractions. They checked it against an independent normalizer (from the FairSpeech project), which gave similar reductions on most datasets but smaller ones on WSJ, CallHome and Switchboard.

blocks.caption: Word-level edit distance divided by reference length. Real evaluations normalize both strings first.

blocks.md: Normalization done right reveals what matters: **robustness across datasets**. The paper compares Whisper Large V2 with a wav2vec 2.0 Large model fine-tuned on LibriSpeech (no language model). Both score 2.7 WER on LibriSpeech test-clean. Across 13 other English datasets, the average is 29.3 for wav2vec 2.0 and 12.8 for Whisper, and the paper reports Whisper making 55.2% fewer errors on average.

blocks.title: Same LibriSpeech score, different robustness (paper Table 2)

scenes.caption: wav2vec 2.0 Large (no LM), trained on LibriSpeech: 2.7 in-distribution, but far worse on crowd-sourced, far-field and conversational audio.
Whisper Large V2, zero-shot: the same 2.7 on LibriSpeech clean, much lower everywhere else. Matching on one benchmark says little about the others.

blocks.md: Only compare WER numbers computed with the same normalizer on the same references. Switching normalizers, or counting *you're* versus *you are* as an error, can move WER more than a model upgrade. For languages written without spaces, character error rate (CER) is used instead.

blocks.question: A reference has 10 words. The aligned hypothesis has 2 substitutions, 1 deletion and 3 insertions. What is the WER?
blocks.explain: WER = (S + D + I) / N = (2 + 1 + 3) / 10 = 60%. Dividing by the hypothesis length (12 words) would give 50%, a common bug. 30% forgets the insertions.

blocks.question: Your new model lowers WER on your test set from 9% to 6%, but you also switched to a normalizer that expands numbers and removes filler words. What should you conclude?
options: The model is 33% better
Nothing yet: rescore the old model with the new normalizer and compare
The old normalizer was wrong, so only the new number counts
WER is meaningless and should be replaced by human judgment
blocks.explain: Two things changed at once. The Whisper paper reports normalization alone moving WER by up to 50% on some datasets. Score both models with the same normalizer before attributing the gain to the model.

lessons.title: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production

blocks.md:
Whisper sees exactly 30 s at a time, but meetings and podcasts run for hours. Cutting at fixed 30 s boundaries would slice words in half. The paper's **buffered long-form** strategy transcribes a 30 s window, then moves the window start (the *seek* position) to the last complete segment's end timestamp predicted by the model. When the window ends mid-segment, the model emits only that segment's start time, and the next window begins there.

This makes the whole transcript depend on the predicted timestamps: "inaccurate transcription in one window may negatively impact transcription in the subsequent windows."

blocks.title: Seeking through 75 s of audio by predicted timestamps

scenes.caption: Illustrative timestamps. Window 1 covers 0 to 30 s. The last complete segment ends at 27.40 s; the speech after it is cut off by the window edge.
Window 2 starts at the seek point, 27.40 s, not at 30 s, so the cut-off segment is transcribed whole. Its last complete segment ends 26.16 s into the window, at 53.56 s.
Window 3 starts at 53.56 s. Only 21.44 s of audio remain, so it is padded with silence to 30 s, the setting where a decoder is most tempted to invent text.
Drift: if window 1 had predicted 28.00 s instead of 27.40 s, window 2 would start 600 ms late and those words would be lost; predicting too early duplicates words. Errors compound window to window.

blocks.md:
The paper lists the long-form failure modes as "getting stuck in repeat loops, not transcribing the first or last few words of an audio segment, or complete hallucination where the model will output a transcript entirely unrelated to the actual audio." Its workarounds, most of which are defaults in `whisper.transcribe` (beam search is the exception: only the command line tool defaults to 5 beams, the Python function decodes greedily unless you pass `beam_size`):

- **Beam search** with 5 beams at temperature 0, which loops less than greedy decoding.
- **Temperature fallback**: if the average token log probability is below -1, or the text's compression ratio is above 2.4 (repetitive text compresses well), retry at temperature 0.2, 0.4 and so on up to 1.0.
- **Silence check**: a no-speech probability above 0.6 together with average log probability below -1 marks the window as silent.
- **Previous-text conditioning** only when the temperature is below 0.5, and the first timestamp forced into 0 to 1 s.

blocks.title: Temperature fallback on a looping output

scenes.caption: Simplified from whisper/transcribe.py. The first attempt uses temperature 0 with beam search.
The decoder looped: Thank you for watching. repeated 10 times is 240 bytes that zlib compresses to 35, a ratio of 6.86.
Retry with sampling at temperature 0.2. This time the text is a normal sentence: ratio 1.26, average log probability -0.4 (illustrative).
No check failed, so the loop stops and keeps this result. A fluent, confident invented sentence would pass these same checks.

blocks.title: Decoding heuristics lower long-form WER (paper Table 7)

scenes.caption: Average WER over seven long-form datasets, adding one heuristic at a time: 11.0 down to 10.0, about a 9% relative cut. Two steps leave the average flat, and the paper notes gains are uneven across datasets.

blocks.md:
**Offline** transcription has the whole file: it can look ahead, use beam search and take as long as it needs. **Streaming** transcription must show words while the person is still talking, and its key metric is *latency*, how long after a word is spoken it appears.

One path is a model built for streaming, such as the recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T, introduced by Graves in 2012), which Google used for streaming on-device recognition in 2018 and which outperformed a conventional CTC-based model in both latency and accuracy in a number of evaluation categories. The other is to wrap an offline model. **Whisper-Streaming** (Macháček, Dabre and Bojar, 2023) re-transcribes a growing audio buffer and applies the **LocalAgreement-2** policy: it confirms only the longest common prefix of the last two transcripts. It reported 3.3 s latency on a long-form test set.

blocks.title: LocalAgreement-2: confirm what two updates agree on

scenes.caption: First update on a short buffer. There is nothing to compare with yet, so nothing is shown to the user.
Second update with more audio: fax became fox. The longest common prefix is the quick brown, so those three words are confirmed.
Third update: fox jumps now appears twice in a row, so it is confirmed. The unstable tail (over the) waits for the next update.
Fourth update confirms over the. Every word waits at least one extra update, which is the latency cost of not showing words that might still change.

blocks.md:
**Hallucination** means text that was never spoken. Whisper trains on silent segments too (target: the no-speech token), yet the paper found the no-speech probability alone is not enough to detect silence. Weak web labels also contain text that is not in the audio, like the speaker names from lesson 2.

The *Careless Whisper* study (Koenecke et al., FAccT 2024) ran 13,140 AphasiaBank audio segments through OpenAI's Whisper API in 2023. Roughly **1%** of transcriptions contained entire hallucinated phrases or sentences, and **38%** of those hallucinations included explicit harms such as invented violence or false authority. Hallucinations were more common for speech with longer non-vocal stretches, such as the pauses typical of aphasia.

Silence is where a language-model decoder is least constrained by audio. Short clips are padded to 30 s, long pauses leave long stretches of nothing, and the decoder can fill them with plausible web-caption text. The repetition and confidence checks do not catch a fluent, confident invented sentence.

Practical mitigations: run voice activity detection (VAD) and only send speech regions to the model; keep the no-speech and log-probability thresholds; set `condition_on_previous_text=False` if loops or timestamp drift appear (the docstring warns about both); try `hallucination_silence_threshold` with word timestamps to skip long silent gaps; and have people review transcripts used for medical or legal decisions.

Long-form and streaming ASR are decoding problems layered on a fixed-window model: the window moves by predicted timestamps, unstable text waits for agreement, and silence must be removed or detected before the decoder invents something to say.

blocks.question: In Whisper-Streaming you raise MinChunkSize, the minimum new audio processed per update. What happens?
options: Latency rises, but each update sees more audio, so quality tends to improve
Latency drops, because fewer updates are needed
Nothing, because LocalAgreement only depends on text
WER rises, because the 30 s window overflows
blocks.explain: The paper describes MinChunkSize as the parameter that controls latency and quality. Bigger chunks mean waiting longer before each update, but each transcription has more context. The paper also found the computationally unaware latency (ignoring compute time) to be about twice the chunk size, since two consecutive updates must agree. Buffers are trimmed at sentence ends to stay near 30 s, so overflow is not the issue.

blocks.question: A clinic transcribes hour-long recordings with long pauses, and reviewers find invented sentences in the quiet parts. Which change targets the cause most directly?
options: Use a larger beam
Run VAD and send only detected speech to the model
Lower the compression-ratio threshold to 1.5
Switch WER normalizers
blocks.explain: The invented text appears where there is no speech for the decoder to follow. Removing non-speech before decoding takes away the empty input the decoder fills. A larger beam or a stricter compression threshold targets loops, not fluent inventions, and a normalizer only changes scoring.

blocks.question: Window 1 predicts its last complete segment ends at 28.00 s, but the speaker actually finished it at 27.40 s and started a new sentence. What does buffered long-form transcription do next?
options: Starts window 2 at 30.00 s, as always
Starts window 2 at 28.00 s and may skip the words spoken between 27.40 and 28.00 s
Re-runs window 1 with a higher temperature
Averages the two timestamps and starts at 27.70 s
blocks.explain: The seek position follows the predicted timestamp, so window 2 starts at 28.00 s and the 600 ms after the true boundary is never transcribed. This is the error propagation between windows that the paper warns about.
